name: Skipcare

lead: Skipcare refers to the trend of skipping skincare steps in favour of a shorter routine. It is the opposite of the long multi-product routines popular on social media, and followers say it saves time and avoids irritation from too many actives.

The appearance payoff is clear skin and an even complexion from a routine people actually keep up. Dermatology sources describe a basic core of gentle cleansing, moisturiser and sun protection, with other products added for specific needs such as acne.

paras: People typically keep a small set of products, often a gentle cleanser, moisturiser and sunscreen, and drop toners, serums or extra steps. Some add a single targeted product for a specific concern.
Low in itself. Dropping a core step such as sunscreen is the point where dermatologists describe a trade-off, and people with conditions such as acne may need targeted products.

chain: A routine that is easier to keep up and less irritating
angle.text: Followers say a short routine covering cleansing, moisturiser and sunscreen is easier to maintain, which is what keeps skin looking even over time.[1]

lead: Skipcare is a term for the trend of leaving steps out of a skincare routine. Its appeal is a shorter, cheaper and lower-effort regimen that still aims at clear, healthy-looking skin.

Dermatological guidance summarised on Wikipedia gives a foundational routine of gentle cleansing, moisturising and sun protection, with additional products reserved for specific clinical needs such as acne.[1] The same source notes that elaborate routines promoted on social media can lead young people to use harsh or unnecessary products, which is the concern minimalist approaches respond to.[1]
Public coverage and research on skipcare under that name are limited; the entry draws on the general literature on skin care routines.

paras: The idea is to reduce the number of products and steps while keeping the ones considered essential. Dermatologists quoted in the general skin care literature name gentle cleansing, moisturising and sun protection as the foundation.[1]

Proponents say long routines can irritate skin and cost more without added benefit, and that a few consistent steps are easier to maintain. Dermatology sources note that products beyond the basics are generally for specific conditions.[1]
No studies found. Skipcare as a trend has not been studied.
